claims.claim: English has four main sentence types — declarative, imperative, interrogative, and exclamatory — and an interrogative sentence is one that asks a question, typically ending with a question mark.
Yes/no questions ask for a yes or no answer and are formed by placing an auxiliary verb (be, do, or have), or the main verb be, or a modal verb before the subject.
When a statement contains no auxiliary, questions in the present and past simple use do, does, or did before the subject, and the main verb returns to its base form (She works → Does she work?).
The verb be does not take do-support in questions: the correct forms are "Are you ready?" and "Is she your sister?", not "Do you be ready?" or "Does she be your sister?".
When a verb phrase contains more than one auxiliary, only the first auxiliary moves before the subject in a question (Has the garden been watered?).
Wh- questions begin with a question word such as what, when, where, who, why, or how (along with which, whose, and the formal whom) and ask for information; the answer cannot be yes or no.

In wh- questions the question word comes first, followed by the auxiliary (or be or modal) before the subject and then the main verb; when the wh- word is itself the subject of the clause, no auxiliary is added and word order stays subject-first (Who called you? vs Who did you call?).

Question tags are short auxiliary-or-be plus pronoun endings added to a statement, and by the polarity rule an affirmative statement takes a negative tag while a negative statement takes an affirmative tag (The bus has left, hasn't it? / The bus hasn't left, has it?).

Indirect questions embed a question inside a frame and keep statement word order in the embedded clause, without inversion or do-support (I want to find out whether the rooms have a shower, from Do the rooms have a shower?).

English softens direct questions in polite situations — for example "May I take your plate, sir?" or "Excuse me, I'm looking for Cathedral Street" rather than a blunt "Where's Cathedral Street?" — and polite question frames are one way to avoid being too direct.

Reference grammars flag patterns such as "What she was eating?", "What art means?", and "Are you agree?" as incorrect; the correct forms invert the auxiliary or add do (What was she eating? / What does art mean? / Do you agree?).

Auxiliary verbs (be, have, do) and modal verbs assist the main verb in expressing tense, aspect, modality, voice, or emphasis, and it is these helpers, not the main verb, that move before the subject in questions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Tag polarity is not absolute in spoken English: Cambridge documents a second tag type with an affirmative main clause and an affirmative tag ("She got the email, did she?"), used with rising intonation when the speaker genuinely does not know the answer.
positions: The polarity rule (affirmative statement → negative tag; negative statement → affirmative tag) is the standard pattern for confirmation questions.
Same-polarity (affirmative + affirmative) tags occur in spoken English with a distinct meaning and rising intonation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the polarity rule as the default pattern and names the affirmative+affirmative tag only as a context-dependent spoken variant, per Cambridge's tag page.

conflictingEvidence.issue: who vs whom: whom is the formal object form, but Cambridge notes it is not normally used in speaking, and everyday English often uses who for both subject and object roles.
positions: Formal written style distinguishes who (subject) from whom (object).
Spoken and informal English generally use who in both roles.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses who throughout for both roles, lists whom as a formal variant, and does not present whom as required in speech.

sourceRecords.title: Questions: yes-no questions (Are you feeling cold?) — English Grammar Today, Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: yes/no questions expect yes or no; formation with auxiliary/modal + subject + main verb; do/does/did when no auxiliary is present (with 'Not: Walk you…?' type warnings); be takes no do; only the first auxiliary moves before the subject.

sourceRecords.title: Questions: wh- questions — English Grammar Today, Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: wh- questions begin with what, when, where, who, whom, which, whose, why, how and ask for information, not yes/no; wh- + auxiliary + subject + main verb; when the wh- word is the subject no auxiliary is used (Who owns this bag? vs Who do you love most?).

sourceRecords.title: Tags — English Grammar Today, Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: tags consist of be, do, or have (or a modal or main be) plus a pronoun subject; the polarity rule — affirmative main clause + negative tag, negative main clause + affirmative tag; do/does/did in tags when the main clause has no auxiliary; same-polarity (type 2) tags as a spoken variant.

sourceRecords.title: Questions: typical errors — English Grammar Today, Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports the common-error claims: wh- word order (Not: What she was eating?), do-support when no auxiliary exists (Not: Are you agree? / What art means?), and that only auxiliary/modal verbs, not main verbs, precede the subject (Not: Where was bought the painting?).

sourceRecords.title: Politeness — English Grammar Today, Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports the claim that English softens or changes direct utterances to avoid being too direct or forceful, with polite question forms such as 'May I take your plate, sir?' and 'Excuse me, I'm looking for Cathedral Street' contrasted with a blunt 'Where's Cathedral Street?'.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports the indirect-question claim: embedded yes/no questions keep statement word order and drop the do auxiliary (I want to find out whether the rooms have a shower, original question Do the rooms have a shower?).
